newsitem.title: FRANCE: Club Med reports loss, Triganos walk out.
newsitem.headline: Club Med reports loss, Triganos walk out.

text.p: The Trigano family which founded Club Mediterranee quit the French resort empire on Friday in a clash with the new management, which reported a 413 million franc ($68.2 million) half-year loss after heavy restructuring charges.

Club Med, whose largest shareholder is now Italy's Agnelli family through their Exor SA holding company, said it wanted to revitalise the company that pioneered all-inclusive, fun-in-the-sun holidays but preserve its culture and concept.

Club Med warned it may take further provisions later this year on top of the 630 million francs in the six months to April 30. But the stock rallied as investors welcomed new chairman Philippe Bourguignon's profit-geared approach.
Bourguignon took over from Serge Trigano in February after rescuing Euro Disney and turning Mickey Mouse's Paris outpost into Europe's top tourist attraction.
Trigano said he and his father Gilbert, who co-founded the firm in 1950, had resigned from the supervisory board after a row with Bourguignon, who heads the management board.
He told Europe 1 radio that its chic holiday villages risked turning into "Mickey (Mouse) clubs" and it was time for the founders to get out.

"There was a certain spirit in this firm, a certain soul based on love, tenderness and generosity. ... I don't know if it will be a Mickey Club or something else but it will certainly be a different club from the past and it's not my club," he said.
"The new team has its own methods which are not mine and there is no place left for a Trigano," he added.
He hinted that the Trigano family planned to launch a rival holiday club chain, addressing new markets such as old people.
Club Med, synonymous with holiday villages for three generations of European tourists, underwent a 820 million franc restructuring in 1995/96 and reported a 743 million franc loss.
It had an operating profit of 84 million francs in the 1997 first half, but the gain was more than cancelled out by 88 million francs in net interest payments.
The company's share rallied 5.21 percent to 442 francs in late trading despite the bourse's CAC-40 index 3.8 percent fall.

"The Triganos focused on the product. Bourguignon sees that it's a good product, but poorly sold," said analyst Antoine Nodet at French brokerage Natexis. He and several other brokers raised their ratings on the stock to outperform.

"The Club has fantastic potential which is under-exploited today due to multiple weaknesses," Bourguignon said in a letter to shareholders. "Club Med is a great brand ...It needs to preserve its culture but change its operating methods."

After cleaning up the balance sheet this year, Club Med will strive by 1999 to lure back customers with attractive prices due to stricter cost control. From 2000 to 2002, it will step up the pace of new resort openings and new products.
"This is a company that is growing, not one that's selling cruise ships, closing vacation villages," Bourguignon said, chiding the Triganos' past retrenchment moves.

Club Med said its modest first-half turnover rise to 3.90 billion francs from 3.81 billion was largely due to a stronger dollar and an increase in prices that offset the negative impact of deconsolidation in South America and of flat demand.
Despite the loss, "the financial situation remains healthy with a financial debt limited to 2.4 billion francs for 3.5 billion francs shareholders' equity," it said.

Trigano was kicked upstairs to head the supervisory board to make way for Bourguignon, who was credited with rescuing Euro Disney after the Paris theme park's disastrous start-up. ($ = 6.056 French Francs)
